# The Betrayal

> The Betrayal (thebetrayal.co.uk) is a party game for 8 to 24 players in one room, best with 8 to 16, played on everyone's own phone in the browser. A few players are secretly the Forsworn; the rest, the Loyal, have one evening to find them. It costs £10 for one party or £20 a month. It is an independent game made in England and is not affiliated with any television programme or broadcaster.

## Key facts

- What it is: a hidden-role (social deduction) party game for adults, "the party game of loyalty and lies". Always written "The Betrayal", with "The".
- Players: 8 to 24 in one room, best with 8 to 16. Nobody sits out, and the host never sees anyone else's role.
- Length: about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 players; an hour to an hour and a quarter for 12 to 16; an hour and a half to two hours for 20 to 24. Classic takes longer: about 3 to 3½ hours for 8 to 12 players.
- What you need: a phone each (any browser; no app to download, no account) and a prize. A TV is optional: a laptop connected or casting to it shows the questions, votes and reveals, with music.
- Joining: guests scan the QR code on the TV, or go to thebetrayal.co.uk/join and type the six-character Table code and their name.
- Prize: set by the host. By default, chocolate coins: one coin for every 100 points the winners take from the Purse.
- Price: a Table is £10 for one party of 8 to 24, open for 48 hours from when its game starts (until then an opened Table waits up to 30 days). A Regular is £20 a month: one booking code that opens a new Table whenever you like, one at a time; cancel any time. Payments by Stripe. Prices include VAT where it applies.
- How to buy: https://thebetrayal.co.uk/buy. The booking code (OATH-XXXX-XXXX) is shown on screen straight after payment; enter it on the home page to open a Table.
- Contact: info@thebetrayal.co.uk or https://thebetrayal.co.uk/contact

## How a game works (Modern, everyone on their own phone)

1. The host opens the Table with their booking code and name; guests join on their phones.
2. The Oath: each phone privately asks its player whether they would like to be Forsworn, then deals the roles. The Forsworn (about one player in four or five: 2 for 8 to 10 players, 3 for 11 to 16, 4 for 17 to 22, 5 for 23 or 24) see each other; nobody else sees anything.
3. Trials: party games played on the phones (quizzes, word games, guessing games, charades where only the actor sees the word, rock-paper-scissors and more; 15 in all, drawing on thousands of questions and prompts). They fill a shared Purse and win Sanctuary, protection from that night.
4. The Reckoning: a few minutes of debate on a timer, then a secret vote on every phone. The player with the most votes is exiled and their role is revealed.
5. Night: the Forsworn choose someone to poison. Everyone else taps a name too, so nobody can tell who is choosing. At dawn the victim, told first in secret on their phone, announces it and gets thirty seconds of last words.
6. Players who are out become Ghosts: they stay at the party, still call each vote, and play most Trials for a Ghosts' score that never touches the Purse.
7. The final starts with five or fewer players (four or fewer with 8, so 8 players get a second night). The survivors decide in secret whether they trust everyone left (one doubt means another vote, without a reveal); then the Unmasking reveals every role. The Loyal win if every Forsworn is gone and take the Purse they built; the Forsworn win if one survives and take what the Purse fell short of its target. The game ends with up to six awards.

Classic is the other way to play every Table, for a longer, more immersive evening of about three hours: a TV with a laptop, one phone for a Keeper who reads the script and doesn't play, blindfolds at night and votes chalked on small boards. Classic also has a Short game of about 2 to 2½ hours for 8 to 10 players.

## Comparisons

- The Betrayal is similar in idea to the TV show The Traitors (hidden traitors, a vote each day, a victim each night), but it is an original game that you play yourselves at home, and it is not connected to The Traitors, the BBC or its makers.
- It is often used as an alternative to a murder mystery party: no scripts, characters or booklets, nobody knows the answer in advance, and it works for any number from 8 to 24.
- Occasions: games nights, birthday parties, Christmas and office parties, hen and stag dos, dinner parties (in Classic, dinner in courses is served between the rounds).

## Playing a traitors-style game at home: quick answers

- How do you play The Traitors at home? A few players are secretly traitors; everyone else tries to find them. Each round there's a challenge, a debate and a secret vote to banish someone, and each night the traitors pick a victim. The loyal players win by banishing every traitor. The Betrayal runs all of this on everyone's phones (an independent, original game, not the official one); https://thebetrayal.co.uk/traitors-at-home explains how to run it by hand too.
- How many traitors for my group? About one player in four or five: 2 traitors for 8 to 10 players, 3 for 11 to 16, 4 for 17 to 22, 5 for 23 or 24.
- Is there a traitors game you can play on your phones? Yes: The Betrayal, for 8 to 24 players in one room, in the phone's browser with no app, £10 a party.
- How long does it take? On phones with The Betrayal, about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 players and up to about two hours for 24. Run by hand, 3 hours or more.
- Ideas for a traitors-themed party: https://thebetrayal.co.uk/traitors-party-ideas

# How to play
These are the rules of The Betrayal, a party game for 8 to 24 players. They cover everything that happens in a game, from the first oath to the last betrayal. You don’t need to learn any of it before you play, because every phone tells its player what to do and when. But if you like to know what you’re buying, here is the whole game.
This page describes the game as most people play it, with everyone on their own phone. For a longer, more immersive evening, there’s Classic, with a Keeper, blindfolds and chalk.

## The idea
A few of your guests are secretly the Forsworn. They are the traitors, and they know who each other are. Everyone else is one of the Loyal, and the Loyal don’t know who anyone is. Every night the Forsworn poison someone, which puts that player out of the game. Every day, everyone votes to throw someone out. The Loyal win if they vote out every Forsworn before the end. The Forsworn win if even one of them is still in the game when it finishes.
In between, you play party games called Trials. They fill a shared prize pot, and they can win you protection from the poison for a night. You argue, you make alliances, and you lie to people you’ve known for years. A game lasts from about 45 minutes to two hours, depending on how many play, so have drinks and snacks ready.

## Joining
The host opens the Table, which is your game for the evening, by entering their booking code and their name. Everyone else scans the QR code on the TV, or goes to thebetrayal.co.uk/join and types the six-character Table code and their name. There’s nothing to install and no account to make. The TV is optional. Without one, the host reads the Table code out from their phone. When everyone has joined, the host taps Start. The game needs at least 8 players.

## Who’s who
The Loyal are most of the players. They don’t know anyone else’s role. Their job is to work out who the Forsworn are and vote them out. They have nothing to go on but what people say, how they vote and their gut feeling.
The Forsworn are about one guest in four or five. Their phones tell them who the other Forsworn are. Each night they secretly choose someone to poison. By day they pretend to be Loyal, steer the vote towards other players, and quietly do badly in the Trials.
The host has a secret role like everyone else and never sees anyone else’s. Their phone also moves the evening on. It shows a button for the next part of the game, and the host taps it when everyone is ready. Before each Trial, the host taps to start it once everyone has heard the rules. The host can also call a break, open the vote early or add a minute to a clock. The game itself chooses the Trials and plans the rounds.
Sometimes a game can’t carry on, for example because a phone dies and nobody remembers who was Forsworn. As a last resort, the host’s tools can then show the roles. The phone asks three times first, and everyone is told at the end that the host looked.
The night begins with the Oath. Every phone asks its player, in secret, whether they would like to be Forsworn. They can say yes, say they’d rather be Loyal, or say either way. The game uses the answers to choose the roles, and it picks volunteers first, but nobody is promised what they asked for. Then each player holds their phone close and looks at their role.
Nobody is told how many Forsworn there are. You only find out as Forsworn are voted out and their roles are shown.

## A round
The game is played in rounds. It plans how many from the number of players, so that the final round starts with five or fewer players left. With 8 players it starts with four or fewer, which gives them a second night. Each round goes like this:

- A Trial. A Trial is a party game played on the phones, such as a quiz, a guessing game or charades. They are all listed below. Each question closes by itself when everyone has answered or the clock runs out. Every Trial adds to the Purse, the shared prize pot. Most Trials also give Sanctuary to the winner, which keeps them safe from the poison that night. The evening opens with Most Likely To, as an icebreaker.
- The Reckoning. This is the debate and the vote. First, everyone argues about who might be Forsworn while a timer runs. The timer gives thirty seconds for each player still in, up to four minutes. Then everyone votes in secret on their phone. The vote closes when everyone has voted, and once all but one have voted, the last player has thirty seconds. The player with the most votes is exiled, which means voted out. If there’s a tie, everyone votes again between the tied players. If that ties too, the game picks one of them at random. While more than sixteen players are left, two players are exiled each time.
- The reveal. Everyone sees whether the exiled player was Forsworn or Loyal. On the way out, the exiled player can type one last line, which the TV shows.
- The night. Everyone looks down at their phone. The Forsworn secretly choose someone to poison, and everyone else taps a name too, so nobody can tell who is really choosing. While twelve or more players are left, the Forsworn choose two people. While twenty or more are left, they choose three. All the Forsworn must choose the same people, so the night waits until they agree. If the clock runs out first, the players chosen most are poisoned. Once the Forsworn agree, the last player still to tap has thirty seconds. A player holding Sanctuary can’t be poisoned. The Forsworn also have a secret chat of their own, under Your role on their phones, which they can use at any time.
- Dawn. This is the morning. The poisoned player finds out first, in secret, on their phone. Then the host shows everyone what happened in the night. The victim was poisoned, which means they are out of the game. They stand up, tell everyone, and get thirty seconds of last words before they leave the table. If everyone once voted them most likely to do something, the TV mentions that too.

The host can call a short break whenever they like. They can also pause the game, which stops every clock, for the doorbell or a top-up of drinks. If someone is taken ill, the host can take them out of the game without anyone learning their role.

## The dead
Nobody goes home when they’re out. Players who are exiled or poisoned become Ghosts. They stay at the party and watch the game on their phones. Ghosts can’t vote. But at every Reckoning they can say who they think should go, and everyone is told which Ghosts guessed right. In many Trials the Ghosts play on for a score of their own. It never touches the Purse, the Trial’s winner or Sanctuary, and the best Ghost of the night can win an award. In The Statue, the Ghosts do their worst to make the living laugh.

## Sanctuary
Sanctuary keeps its holder safe from the poison for one night. It’s the prize in most Trials. At most a quarter of the players can hold it at the same time. Before the game starts, the host chooses whether Sanctuary is public or secret. If it’s public, everyone is told who won it. If it’s secret, only the winner knows they’re safe. A Forsworn who wins a secret Sanctuary gets nothing, and nobody else knows.

## Twists
Twists are surprises that change the game for a moment. Each one comes once in the evening, and the phones explain it when it happens. The host can switch them all off before the start, for a simpler first game.

- The Casting Vote comes about halfway through. The winner of that Trial gets it instead of Sanctuary, and nobody else knows who has it. It’s a secret tie-breaker. If a Reckoning ties and its holder voted for one of the tied players, their vote decides it.
- In the Temptation, everyone secretly chooses PURSE or SELF. If exactly one person chooses SELF, they get Sanctuary and the Purse grows. If nobody chooses SELF, the Purse grows by double. If two or more choose SELF, nobody gets Sanctuary and the Purse shrinks.
- The Crown comes in the last round before the final, and everyone is told who wins it. It gives its holder Sanctuary that night. Also, once, at a Reckoning, the holder can lay it down to be safe from that vote.
- The Confessor comes in the final. The winner of that Trial is told, in secret, the name of one Forsworn who is still playing.

## The Purse
The Purse is the shared prize pot. Every Trial adds to it, up to a target, and the better everyone plays, the more goes in. The Trial in the final plays for everything the Purse is still missing, so a perfect final fills it. Some Trials are knockouts, where players drop out until one is left: Rock Paper Scissors Royale, One Leg and The Statue. They have a winner but no score for the whole group, so they add half their share.
The winners take the Purse at the end. If the Loyal win, they take what they built. If the Forsworn win, they take what it fell short of the target. So every point the Forsworn quietly lose is a point for them. Each wrong answer from a Forsworn takes points out of the Purse. Everyone hears how many wrong answers there were, but never whose. This doesn’t apply to the Rapid Quiz’s brutal questions, which beat most people. A Loyal player’s wrong answers cost nothing, so a shrinking Purse is a clue.
There is also a real prize, chosen by the host. Make it something worth lying to your friends for. If the host doesn’t choose one, it’s chocolate coins, one for every 100 points the winners take from the Purse. The host can also set better prizes for a fuller Purse. If the Forsworn win, it works the other way round, so an emptier Purse wins them a better prize. The players know that the Purse decides the prize, but not what the prize will be.

## The end game
The last round is the final. It starts when five or fewer players are left, or four or fewer in a game of 8. There is no night in the final.

- A last Trial. It plays for everything the Purse is still missing, and perhaps something more. There’s no Sanctuary in the final, because there is no night left to survive.
- The Reckoning, without reveals. Everyone votes a player out, but this time their role is not shown.
- Trust or Doubt. When four or fewer are left, each player still in makes a secret choice on their phone. They choose TRUST if they believe every Forsworn is gone, or DOUBT if not. Once all but one have chosen, the last player has thirty seconds, and no answer counts as DOUBT. The game only ends if everyone chooses TRUST. Otherwise it’s back to the Reckoning for another exile, then another Trust or Doubt. If only two players are left, the game ends anyway.
- The Unmasking. One by one, the roles of the last players are shown. If only Loyal are left, the Loyal win and share the Purse. If a Forsworn is still in the game, the Forsworn win and take what the Purse fell short.
- The last betrayal. If two or more Forsworn are left, each one secretly chooses HONOUR or BETRAY. If they all choose HONOUR, they share the winnings. If one chooses BETRAY, they take everything. If two or more choose BETRAY, nobody gets anything.
- The awards. Everyone’s role is shown. Then come up to six awards for the night, such as The Grand Deceiver, The Sharpest Eye, Barking Up the Wrong Tree and The Ghost Who Saw.

## Trials
The game picks the Trials in a random order, so no two evenings are the same.

- Most Likely To  Every phone shows a prompt. Vote for the person it fits best, then see who everyone chose. There’s no prize, only a reputation.
- Rapid Quiz  Fifteen questions: five easy, five medium and five brutal. Type your answer before the clock runs out. You get a point for every right answer, and one more if you’re the fastest.
- Longest Word  You get twelve letters. Type the longest real word you can make from them.
- Closest Guess  Each question has a number for its answer. Type your guess, and the closest guesses score.
- Memory Wall  Twelve words appear, then disappear. Type every one you can remember.
- Snap  A symbol changes every few seconds. When it matches the one before, tap SNAP. A wrong tap counts against you.
- Rock Paper Scissors Royale  Players are paired up at random, and each pair plays rock, paper, scissors on their phones. Lose and you’re out. It goes on until one player is left.
- One Leg  Everyone stands on one leg. If your other foot touches the floor, tap the button on your phone to say you’re out. The last one standing wins.
- Screen Charades  One player at a time gets a secret word on their phone and acts it out. When someone guesses it, the actor taps their name.
- Hum It  Like charades, but your phone gives you a song to hum.
- Draw It  Like charades, but you draw the word on paper, on a board or in the air. You can’t use letters or numbers.
- The Statue  The players still in the game freeze like statues. The Ghosts can do anything except touch them to make them move or laugh.
- Two Truths and a Lie  One player says three things about themselves. Two are true and one is a lie. Everyone else votes on their phone for the lie.
- Higher or Lower  You see a question and a number. Is the real answer higher or lower than that number?
- What Changed?  Twelve symbols appear, then disappear. When they come back, something is different. Tap what changed. The first right answer scores double.

The quiz, charades, songs, pictures and guessing games draw on a bank of thousands of questions and prompts, and nothing repeats within a game.

## Classic: the longer, more immersive evening
Every Table can also be played Classic, and you choose which way to play when you open it. It’s the same game, run differently, and it takes about 3 to 3½ hours for 8 to 12 players. Here is what changes:

- A Keeper runs it. The Keeper is the person who runs the game from one phone and reads its lines aloud, like a presenter. They know who the Forsworn are, so they don’t play. The host can still play. They plan the game, then hand the phone to a friend, who becomes the Keeper.
- The Oath is sworn blindfolded. The Keeper walks behind the chairs, and a tap on the shoulder makes someone Forsworn. Then the Forsworn take off their blindfolds to see each other.
- Votes are chalked on small boards. The boards are turned round one at a time, and the TV keeps count. In the Trials, players shout or chalk their answers.
- Nights are blindfolded. The Keeper wakes the Forsworn, who point to their victim in silence. Then the Keeper taps the victim, who reads the screen and says nothing until dawn.
- The Keeper chooses more. They choose how many rounds to play, which Trials, whether there are Ghosts, and whether to have an Interval, a 10-minute break before the vote. There are extra twists too, such as a whispered offer to change sides and secret tasks for the Forsworn. If the Forsworn betray each other at the end, the winnings can pass to the Ghosts who named a Forsworn.
- Dinner fits in. If you switch on dinner in courses, the game makes time for a starter early on, the main course mid-game, and dessert just before the final.
- You need a TV for Classic, because it’s where the players see the game.

## What you need

- 8 to 24 players. 8 to 16 is the sweet spot.
- Between 45 minutes and two hours. It takes about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 players, an hour to an hour and a quarter for 12 to 16, and an hour and a half to two hours for 20 to 24. Classic takes longer, about 3 to 3½ hours for 8 to 12. When the Keeper sets up a Classic game, their phone gives an estimate for your group.
- A prize, such as a bag of chocolate coins.
- A phone each. A TV is optional, but it makes the game a show. Connect a laptop to it, or cast to it.
- For Classic, you need a TV with a laptop connected or casting to it, and a phone for the Keeper. Every guest needs a blindfold, and sleep masks work well. Every guest also needs a small chalkboard and chalk, or a whiteboard and pen.

In short, The Betrayal is a hidden-role party game for 8 to 24 players in one room. It’s best with 8 to 16, and it’s played on everyone’s own phone with no app to install. A game takes about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 players, and up to about two hours for 24. A Table costs £10 for one party, or £20 a month as a Regular.

# How to host a traitors-style game at home
A traitors-style game needs no set and no camera crew. A few players are secretly traitors, everyone else tries to find them, the group votes someone out each day, and the traitors pick someone off each night. This guide is how to run one for 8 to 24 friends in your own home: by hand, or the easy way on everyone’s phones.
The Traitors is a BBC programme. This guide and The Betrayal are independent. They are not affiliated with, endorsed by or connected to the programme, the BBC or its makers. The Betrayal is an original party game.
Short of time? The Betrayal runs a traitors-style game on everyone’s phones for you, for 8 to 24 players. The phones handle the secret roles, the challenges, the vote and the night, so the host plays too. It costs £10 for the whole party, with nothing to print or prepare. How it works · Book a Table

## What is a traitors-style game?
It’s a hidden-role game, also called a social deduction game. The idea is much older than television. Parlour games like Mafia, first played in Moscow in the 1980s, and Werewolf work the same way. A small group of players are secretly on the other side. They know each other, but nobody else knows them. The majority win by voting every traitor out. The traitors win if even one of them survives to the end.
What makes it work at a party is that nobody can prove anything. There is only what people say, how they vote and how they look when they say it. It suits adults who like a debate, a bluff and a quiet grudge, and it works best with 8 or more people.

## What you need

- 8 to 24 people. With fewer than 8, the game is over in a couple of rounds. With more than 24, the votes take too long.
- A way to deal roles in secret. Playing cards work, as explained below, or a phone each if you use an app.
- A way to vote in secret. Slips of paper and pens, small whiteboards, or phones.
- A way to hide the night. Everyone closes their eyes, and sleep masks stop peeking.
- A few party games for the day: a quiz, charades, a guessing game.
- A prize. Chocolate coins are traditional, because they can be counted, shared out and fought over.
- Time. By hand, allow about 3 to 3½ hours for 8 to 12 players. On phones, where the games are timed and scored for you, it’s 45 minutes to an hour and a quarter.

## How many traitors?
About one player in four or five should be a traitor. With too few, they’re caught by the second vote. With too many, the loyal players never stand a chance. These are the numbers The Betrayal deals:

Players | Traitors

8 to 10 | 2
11 to 16 | 3
17 to 22 | 4
23 or 24 | 5

Don’t tell the players how many traitors there are. Not knowing is half the fun, because every exile raises the question of whether that was the last one.

## The roles
The traitors know who the other traitors are. By day they act loyal, steer the vote towards innocent players and quietly lose the games. By night they choose who goes.
The loyal players are everyone else. They know only their own role. They win by finding and voting out every traitor.
The host runs the evening. If you run the game by hand, whoever deals the roles and runs the night knows who the traitors are, so they can’t play. That’s the biggest drawback of doing it by hand: someone has to sit it out.
Players who are out stay at the party. Let them watch, heckle and guess. They often enjoy the rest of the night more than anyone.

## How the game runs

- Deal the roles in secret. Take one playing card per player: a black card for each traitor and a red card for everyone else. Shuffle, deal face down, and have everyone look at theirs without showing anyone.
- Let the traitors find each other. Everyone closes their eyes. The host says “Traitors, open your eyes.” They look around, see each other, and close their eyes again. Then everyone opens their eyes.
- Play a game for the prize pot. A quiz round, charades, a guessing game. Every win adds to a shared pot. The traitors will try to lose without being seen to lose.
- Hold the vote. Give the table a few minutes to argue on a timer, then everyone writes one name in secret. Reveal the votes together. The player with the most votes is out and reveals whether they were a traitor.
- Night falls. Everyone closes their eyes. The host wakes the traitors, who silently point at a victim, then go back to sleep.
- Dawn. Everyone opens their eyes and the host names the victim. Give them thirty seconds of last words before they leave the table.
- Repeat a game, a vote and a night each round, until about five players are left.
- The final and the reveal. The last players decide whether they trust everyone left. If they all do, turn over every card. If only loyal players remain, they win the pot. If a traitor is still at the table, the traitors win. If anyone doubts, hold another vote, this time without showing the role, and ask again.

## Getting the vote right

- Keep it secret until the reveal. If people vote out loud one by one, the last few simply follow the crowd. Written votes, turned over together or one at a time, make every vote count.
- Put the debate on a clock. Five minutes is plenty. The best accusations come in the last thirty seconds.
- Decide ties in advance. A quick revote between the tied players, then a coin toss if it ties again.
- Show the role of whoever goes. It’s the only hard evidence anyone gets all night, and it makes the next vote sharper.

## Making the night work
The night is where most home games go wrong: a creaking chair or a rustle of movement gives the traitors away. Keep the room quiet, ask everyone to put their heads down, and make the traitors point, not whisper. While 12 or more players are left, let the traitors choose two victims a night so the game doesn’t drag.
On phones it’s easier: if everyone taps a name on their screen at night, nobody can tell who is really choosing. That’s how The Betrayal does it.

## Prizes
A prize makes people lie properly. Put a pot of chocolate coins in the middle and add to it every time the group wins a game. If the loyal players win, they share the pot. For a nastier twist, set a target. If the traitors win, they take what the pot fell short of it, so every game they quietly lost was money in their pocket.

## How long it takes
By hand, a round of a game, the vote and the night takes about 30 to 40 minutes. For 8 to 12 players, plan on about 3 to 3½ hours in all. Bigger groups need more rounds: about 4¼ hours for 16, and 5 to 6 hours for 20 and up. A sample evening for ten:

7.30pm | Arrivals and drinks
7.45pm | The rules, then the roles are dealt
8pm | Round one: a game, the vote, the night
8.40pm to 10pm | Two or three more rounds, with a break for food if you’re eating
10pm | The final with five left
10.45pm | The reveal, the prize and the post-mortem

## Tips for the host

- Explain the rules once, briefly, before the roles are dealt. Everything else can be learnt as you go.
- Plan the games before anyone arrives. A pile of quiz questions and charades cards saves a lot of dead air.
- Keep it moving. Timers for the debate, the vote and the last words stop one loud guest running the evening.
- Sit in a circle, so everyone can see everyone’s face at the vote.
- Keep the out players involved. Let them guess who the traitors are and see who was right at the end.
- Make the ending an event. Turn the roles over one at a time. It’s the moment people talk about afterwards.

## The easy way: play The Betrayal
The Betrayal is a party game that runs all of this for you on everyone’s own phone, so nobody has to sit out. Guests scan a QR code on the TV or go to thebetrayal.co.uk/join. There’s no app to install and no account to make. In The Betrayal, the traitors are called the Forsworn, and everyone else is called the Loyal.

- Each phone gives its player a secret role. The Forsworn see who each other are, and nobody else sees anything.
- There are fifteen Trials, which are party games played on the phones, such as quizzes, charades where only the actor sees the word, word games and guessing games. The game times and scores them for you, and they fill a shared prize pot called the Purse.
- At the Reckoning, the game’s debate and vote, everyone votes in secret on their phone. Then everyone learns whether the exiled player was Forsworn or Loyal.
- At night everyone taps a name, so nobody can tell who is choosing. The victim learns they were poisoned in secret, then announces it at dawn.
- The game plans its own rounds for your group size, up to 24 players. It ends with the Unmasking, when every role is shown, and up to six awards.

It costs £10 for one party, or £20 a month as a Regular. One party is a Table, which stays open for 48 hours from when the game starts. A TV makes it a show but is optional. On the phones, a game takes about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 players. For a longer, more immersive evening, every Table can also be played Classic, with blindfolds, chalkboards and a Keeper who reads the script.

Planning the whole evening, from the invitations to the food? See traitors party ideas.

## Questions

### How many traitors should there be?
About one player in four or five: 2 traitors for 8 to 10 players, 3 for 11 to 16, 4 for 17 to 22, and 5 for 23 or 24.

### Can the host play too?
Not if you run the game by hand, because whoever runs the night knows who the traitors are. If the game runs on phones, as The Betrayal does, the host plays like everyone else and never sees a role.

### What is the minimum number of players?
Eight is the practical minimum for a full evening, and The Betrayal needs at least 8. With fewer, the game ends after a couple of rounds.

### Do we need a TV?
No. By hand you need only cards, paper and pens. With The Betrayal, a TV shows the questions, the votes and the reveals, with music, but everything can be played on the phones alone.

### Is The Betrayal the official game of The Traitors?
No. The Betrayal is an independent, original party game made in England. It isn’t affiliated with, endorsed by or connected to The Traitors, the BBC or any other television programme or broadcaster.

# Traitors party ideas
A traitors-themed party is a dinner party with a secret: a few of your guests are traitors, and by the end of the night everyone else has to work out who. Here’s how to throw one for 8 to 24 friends, from the invitations to the final reveal.
The Traitors is a BBC programme. This page and The Betrayal are independent. They are not affiliated with, endorsed by or connected to the programme, the BBC or its makers. The Betrayal is an original party game.

## The plan in one minute

- Guests: 8 to 24 adults. 8 to 16 is the sweet spot.
- Dress code: dark and dramatic, such as cloaks, capes, tweed, black tie or anything a castle would approve of.
- The room: one long table, low light and candles.
- Food: a banquet you can share, then the game after dinner.
- The game: secret roles, a vote each round and a victim each night. Run it by hand, or let everyone’s phones run it for you.
- The prize: a pot the loyal players win if they catch every traitor.

## Invitations
Tell guests the theme and the dress code, and that there will be a game with secret roles, but nothing more. The suspense starts on the doorstep. Something like:
You are summoned to a night of loyalty and lies. Dress for a castle. Some of you will be traitors. Trust nobody.
Ask everyone to come with a charged phone if you’ll play on phones. Give a firm start time too, because the game works best when everyone is there for the first vote.

## Dress code
Dark colours, capes and cloaks, tweed and tartan, long coats, gloves and the odd dramatic hat. A few spare cloaks or scarves by the door mean nobody feels left out. Some hosts give the eventual winners a sash or a badge to wear for the rest of the night.

## Setting the room

- One long table where everyone can see each other’s faces. Accusations land better across a table.
- Low lights, candles and a dark tablecloth. Use battery candles if there are drinks about.
- A TV for the scores and the reveals, if you have one. It turns the game into a show for the room.
- Somewhere for the traitors to meet unseen, if you’re playing by hand. On phones they don’t need it, because their phones tell them who their fellow traitors are.

## Food and drink
Go for a banquet: sharing boards, pies, a big stew or a roast, and bread to tear. Keep it easy to eat while talking, because there will be a lot of talking. A dark “poisoned” cocktail is a good welcome drink, such as blackberry and gin, or a blackcurrant mocktail. Something warm works in winter. Plan the game for after the main course, or play between courses with the plates cleared for each vote.

## The game
About one guest in four or five is secretly a traitor: 2 for 8 to 10 players, 3 for 11 to 16, 4 for 17 to 22 and 5 for 23 or 24. The traitors know each other. Each round there’s a challenge, then everyone debates and votes someone out, then at night the traitors choose a victim. The loyal players win if they vote out every traitor. The traitors win if even one survives to the end.
You can run it by hand, with role cards and a host who doesn’t play. Our guide to hosting a traitors-style game at home has the rules, the numbers and a timetable. By hand, plan on about 3 to 3½ hours for 8 to 12 players.
Or let the phones run it. The Betrayal is a traitors-style party game played on everyone’s own phone, so the host plays too. The phones deal the secret roles, run the challenges, take the secret votes and handle the night, for 8 to 24 players, with no app to install. A game takes about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 players and up to about two hours for 24. It’s £10 for the whole party.
For a dinner party with phones away, every Table can also be played Classic. In Classic, a Keeper runs the game from one phone and reads its lines aloud. Guests wear blindfolds at night, and dinner can be served in courses between the rounds.

## Prizes
Put up a prize pot. Chocolate coins are the classic choice. The loyal players win the pot if they catch every traitor, and if a traitor survives, the traitors share it instead. Small awards at the end go down well too, such as the best liar, the worst accuser and the most suspicious face. The Betrayal hands out up to six of its own.

## A Christmas traitors party
The theme works brilliantly for Christmas. It’s a game everyone plays at once, so nobody is left watching from the sofa. Swap the cloaks for festive jumpers if you like, serve mulled wine as the “poison” and play after Christmas dinner. For an office party, play on phones. It works for teams of 8 to 24 and needs no setting up beyond a TV, if you have one. Colleagues who’ve never met learn a lot about each other in an hour.

## Questions

### How many people do you need for a traitors party?
At least 8, and up to 24. The game is at its best with 8 to 16, when everyone gets a say in every vote.

### How long does the game take?
Played on phones with The Betrayal, about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 players, an hour to an hour and a quarter for 12 to 16, and an hour and a half to two hours for 20 to 24. Run by hand, allow 3 hours or more.

### Do guests need to download an app?
No. With The Betrayal everyone plays in their phone’s browser, with no app to install and no account to make.

### Is this the official Traitors game?
No. The Betrayal is an original party game, independent of the TV programme, the BBC and its makers.

# Party games for large groups of adults
Most party games are built for four to six people. Past eight, half the room ends up waiting for a turn. The Betrayal is a party game made for large groups of 8 to 24 adults in one room. Everyone plays at once, on their own phone, from start to finish.

## What makes a good game for a big group

- Everyone plays at the same time. Nobody should spend twenty minutes watching someone else’s turn.
- It’s easy to join. No rulebook to read in advance, no app to download, no accounts. In The Betrayal, guests scan a QR code or go to thebetrayal.co.uk/join and type a code and their name.
- Nobody has to run it. A game that needs a quizmaster or a narrator costs you a guest. The Betrayal plans and runs itself, so nobody sits out.
- It gets people talking to each other, not just to a screen. The best large-group games give the room something to argue about.
- It’s the right length. A big group takes a while to settle, so a game that’s over in twenty minutes leaves you looking for the next one. A game that runs past midnight loses people. For a big group, The Betrayal takes an hour or two.

## How The Betrayal works
At the start, every phone asks its player a private question: would you like to be Forsworn? A few players become the Forsworn, the secret traitors, and they know who each other are. Everyone else is Loyal, and they have one evening to find the Forsworn.
Each round, the group plays a Trial, which is a party game on the phones. It might be a quiz, charades where only the actor sees the word, a word game, a guessing game or rock, paper, scissors. Trials fill a shared prize pot called the Purse. The winner of a Trial usually gets Sanctuary, which keeps them safe from the Forsworn that night. Then comes the Reckoning. Everyone argues for a few minutes about who might be Forsworn, then votes in secret on their phone. The player with the most votes is exiled, which means voted out. At night the Forsworn secretly choose someone to poison. Everyone else taps their phone too, so nobody can tell who is choosing. At the end comes the Unmasking, when every role is shown, then the prize and up to six awards. The rules have the whole game, and the tour shows it screen by screen.

## How the size of the group changes the game
The Betrayal takes 8 to 24 players and is at its best with 8 to 16. It plans its own rounds for your group, so that the final round starts with five or fewer players left, or four in a game of 8. Bigger groups get more Forsworn, more exiles and more poisonings, and a longer game. The numbers go down as players drop out:

Players | Forsworn | Poisoned each night, at first | About how long

8 to 10 | 2 | one | about 45 minutes
11 or 12 | 3 | one | about an hour
13 to 16 | 3 | two | 1 to 1½ hours
17 to 24 | 4, or 5 with 23 or 24 | two, or three with 22 or more. While more than 16 are left, two players are exiled at each vote. | 1½ to 2 hours

Classic, the longer way to play with a Keeper, takes about 3 to 3½ hours for 8 to 12 players.

## Which parties it suits

### Christmas parties and office dos
An office Christmas party game has to work for people who don’t all know each other, in a room that’s often too big for a board game. The Betrayal needs only a phone each, and a big screen or projector if the venue has one. Colleagues discover a talent for lying that nobody suspected. Keep it friendly by choosing a prize everyone would like to win. People who are out become Ghosts, so they can still guess who goes at each vote and play many of the Trials.
All through December, the quiz asks fifteen Christmas questions, from the Twelve Days to Die Hard. Most Likely To goes festive too, with prompts like who’ll eat all the mince pies and who’s on the naughty list.

### Birthday parties for adults
For a birthday with a houseful of friends, it gives the evening a shape: drinks, the Oath, a few rounds and a reveal to finish. Make the birthday guest the host. They open the Table on their phone and still get a secret role like everyone else.

### Hen and stag parties
A hen or stag do mixes friends from different parts of someone’s life. A game of secret roles and accusations gets them talking fast. The awards at the end, such as The Grand Deceiver and The Sharpest Eye, give everyone a story for the next day.

### Games nights
If your games night has outgrown the board games on the shelf, The Betrayal is the one to bring out when twelve people turn up. Everyone plays in their browser, so there’s nothing to set up beyond sharing the code.

### Dinner parties
Play it before or after you eat. On the phones, a game for ten takes about 45 minutes. For a slower evening built around the meal, play Classic. A Keeper runs the game from one phone, and dinner in courses fits between the rounds.

## An alternative to a murder mystery party
A murder mystery party is a lot of work for the host. There are characters to cast weeks ahead, costumes, booklets to read, a script to follow, and a solution that one person already knows. The Betrayal gives you the same suspicion and the same body count at the table, with none of the homework:

- No scripts and no characters. Everyone plays themselves, and the lies are their own.
- Nobody knows the answer in advance, including the host. The Forsworn are chosen at the table, on the night.
- Any number from 8 to 24. There’s no fixed cast, so a late arrival or a cancellation doesn’t spoil anything.
- You can play it again. The roles change every game, and the Trials draw on thousands of questions and prompts, so nothing repeats in a game.
- It’s a game, with a winner. The Loyal win if they find every Forsworn. The Forsworn win if one of them survives.

Nobody is murdered, exactly. The Forsworn poison someone each night, and the victim finds out in secret on their phone before telling everyone at dawn.

## What you need

- 8 to 24 people, and between 45 minutes and two hours. It takes about 45 minutes for 8 to 10 people, and up to about two hours for 24.
- A phone each, with a browser. There’s no app to download and no account to make.
- A prize. Unless you choose something else, it’s chocolate coins, one for every 100 points the winners take from the Purse.
- A TV if you have one, with a laptop connected or casting to it. It puts the questions, votes and reveals on the big screen, with music, but it’s optional.

A Table costs £10 for one party of 8 to 24 players, and stays open for 48 hours from when the game starts. A Regular pays £20 a month and can start a new Table whenever they like. For a longer, more immersive evening, every Table can also be played Classic, with a Keeper, blindfolds and chalkboards.
